Cody Carbone says the banks tanked a bill they needed, and got nothing

"I will always be perplexed by their strategy. From the beginning the banks have said, we want to tank this bill, we don't like this stablecoin reward provision. "The banks get the status quo now that the bill has failed, which means rewards can thrive. I already saw that Coinbase has upped the reward for Coinbase One members. I wouldn't be surprised if every exchange starts upping the rewards. The status quo now exists and continues and will probably thrive, and the banks get nothing."

"Even put the stablecoin reward piece aside, the banks needed this bill. There is a huge section in the banking title about permitted activities that banks can now do with digital assets. Allows them to interact with permissionless blockchains for the first time."

"They were not willing to compromise, because they thought they could get their way and this bill would still pass. And now there's no bill, and now they have to take their ball and go home."

"Three Republicans voted no. If you ask all three, it was because of the banks. They felt like they were hearing from their community banks at home that this was going to cause deposit flight, lending concerns."

Tokenized stocks are arriving onchain faster than DeFi can put them to work.

The value of distributed tokenized stocks is approaching $3B after growing nearly tenfold since the start of 2025. Securitize's SECZ is the largest individual tokenized stock by value. Strategy and Circle account for three of the next four largest products.

Trading and lending give investors ways to use tokenized stocks without moving their capital back through traditional markets. Keeping that capital onchain can support deeper markets and tighter pricing.

The next phase will depend less on how many stocks are tokenized and more on what investors can do with them once they arrive.

thread_tweets.text:

Which one should the Fed use? The one the Fed targets: PCE.

And that measure suggests hiking was appropriate.
---
CPI weights come primarily from the BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey and measure what households spend out of pocket.

PCE weights come primarily from BEA business surveys and national-accounts data. They measure the broader set of goods and services consumed by households—including health care and other services paid for on their behalf by employers or the government.

PCE also adjusts its weights more quickly as spending patterns change. That makes it broader and more responsive to substitution, which is why the Fed prefers it.
---
Neither measure is “wrong.” 

CPI says housing-heavy, out-of-pocket inflation is cooling. OER has slowed to 3.06% and rent to 2.75%.

PCE says broader inflation, especially away from housing, is strengthening.

So the two measures are telling us different things:

* Housing inflation is cooling.
* Broader service inflation is not.

For households, CPI may better capture the inflation they experience directly. But for the Fed, core PCE at 3.3% and rising is the more relevant signal, and it supports a hike.
